name: Skull
description: The 22 bones of the skull plus the hyoid: cranial bones, facial bones and the mandible.

source.attribution: BodyParts3D, (c) The Database Center for Life Science, licensed under CC Attribution-Share Alike 2.1 Japan
source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved). Shapes simplified for the web only.
source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, meshes simplified with quadric decimation for web delivery, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred, one node per structure. Structures marked "merged" are the union of several BodyParts3D meshes (e.g. the parts of one muscle); structures with a "component" take one connected part of a BodyParts3D mesh, chosen by position.

groups.label: Skull
groups.tip: The skull has 22 bones: eight around the brain and 14 in the face. Most meet at locked seams called sutures, and the hyoid is counted separately.

groups.label: Cranial bones (neurocranium)
groups.tip: Old People From Texas Eat Spiders names the eight cranial bones: occipital, two parietals, frontal, two temporals, ethmoid and sphenoid.

groups.label: Facial bones (viscerocranium)
groups.tip: Virgil Can Not Make My Pet Zebra Laugh names the 14 facial bones. Only the vomer and mandible come as singles, the rest come in pairs.

groups.label: Mandible and hyoid
groups.tip: The mandible is the only skull bone that moves freely, every time you talk or chew. The hyoid below it floats alone, touching no other bone.

content.origin: From the Latin word frons, meaning forehead. It is the bone at the front of your head.
content.location: Behind your forehead, forming the roof of both eye sockets. It meets the two parietal bones along the coronal suture, a seam across the top of the head.
content.description: A curved shell of bone, like the front of a helmet. Inside it, just above your eyebrows, are two air spaces called the frontal sinuses.
content.function: It guards the front of your brain, the part that plans and decides. It also shapes your forehead and forms the top rim of each eye socket.
content.mnemonic: Frontal and forehead both start with F, and both sit at the front.
content.clinical: The frontal sinuses can get infected and blocked. This gives pain above the eyes that often gets worse when you bend forward.
content.hint: The single bone behind the forehead, forming the roof of both eye sockets.

questions.text: Which seam joins the frontal bone to the two parietal bones?
questions.explanation: The coronal suture runs across the top of your head, like a headband, between the frontal and parietal bones.

questions.text: Sinus pain just above the eyebrows most likely comes from a sinus in which bone?
questions.explanation: The frontal sinuses sit inside the frontal bone, just above your eyebrows.

content.origin: From the Latin occiput, the back of the head. Put your hand on the back of your head and you are touching it.
content.location: At the back and base of your skull. It meets the parietal bones at the lambdoid suture and sits on top of the atlas, the first neck bone.
content.description: A curved, cup-like bone with a big hole in its base, the foramen magnum. Two smooth knuckles sit beside the hole, and a bump sticks out at the back.
content.function: It guards the back of your brain. The spinal cord passes through its big hole, and its knuckles rock on the atlas when you nod.
content.mnemonic: The Occipital bone Occupies the back of the head and Opens into the foramen magnum.
content.clinical: If pressure builds up inside the skull, the brainstem can be pushed down through the big hole. This is called coning, and it is life threatening.
content.hint: Look at the back and base of the skull for the bone with the big hole where the spinal cord passes.

questions.text: What is the large hole in the occipital bone called?
questions.explanation: Foramen magnum means great hole. The spinal cord passes through it to join the brainstem.

questions.text: The knuckles on the occipital bone, the condyles, form a joint with which bone?
questions.explanation: The occipital condyles rest on the atlas, C1. This joint lets you nod yes.

content.origin: From the Greek word for a wedge. It is wedged in among the other bones of the skull base.
content.location: In the middle of the skull base, right behind your eyes. Its wings reach out to the sides of your head at the temples.
content.description: Shaped like a butterfly or bat, with a body in the middle and wings spreading out. On top of the body is a saddle-shaped dip called the sella turcica.
content.function: It locks the skull and face bones together and forms part of the eye sockets. Its saddle cradles the pituitary gland, and chewing muscles pull on it.
content.mnemonic: Think of the sphenoid as the keystone of the skull, a butterfly with the pituitary sitting in its saddle.
content.clinical: Surgeons can reach a pituitary tumour through the nose and the sphenoid sinus. This avoids opening the skull.
content.hint: A butterfly-shaped bone in the middle of the skull base, with a saddle that holds a small gland.

questions.text: Which gland sits in the saddle, or sella turcica, of the sphenoid bone?
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland, the body's master gland, sits snugly in this saddle-shaped dip.

questions.text: The name sphenoid comes from the Greek word for what?
questions.explanation: Sphen means wedge. The sphenoid is wedged in the middle of the skull base.

content.origin: From the Greek word for a sieve. Part of it is full of tiny holes, like a kitchen sieve.
content.location: Deep in the middle of your face, between your eye sockets and behind your nose. It forms the roof of the nose.
content.description: A light, box-like bone full of small air pockets. Its roof is a flat plate peppered with tiny holes, called the cribriform plate.
content.function: It builds the roof and upper walls of your nose and part of each eye socket. Smell nerves pass up through its tiny holes to reach your brain.
content.mnemonic: Ethmoid means sieve. Your smell nerves sieve through its holes.
content.clinical: A break in the thin, holey plate can tear the brain's lining. Clear brain fluid may then drip from the nose, and the sense of smell can be lost.
content.hint: A light, sieve-like bone between the eye sockets that forms the roof of the nose.

questions.text: Which nerve fibres pass through the tiny holes of the ethmoid bone?
questions.explanation: The olfactory fibres carry smell from your nose up through the cribriform plate to your brain.

questions.text: Clear fluid dripping from the nose after a head injury suggests a break in which part?
questions.explanation: A broken cribriform plate can tear the brain's lining and let brain fluid leak into the nose.

content.origin: From the Latin word paries, meaning a wall. The two parietal bones are the side walls of your skull.
content.location: The upper right side and roof of your skull, above the right ear. It sits behind the frontal bone and in front of the occipital bone.
content.description: A big, curved, roughly square plate, like a roof tile. It meets its partner along the top of the head, at the sagittal suture.
content.function: It forms much of the roof and right wall of your skull. It guards the part of the brain that makes sense of touch and space.
content.mnemonic: Parietal sounds like partition, a wall. The two parietal bones are the walls and roof of the brain's house.
content.clinical: A baby has a soft spot where the two parietal bones meet the frontal bone. A sunken soft spot can mean dehydration, and a bulging one raised pressure.
content.hint: A large curved plate forming the roof and right side wall of the skull, meeting its partner along the midline seam.

questions.text: Which seam joins the right and left parietal bones?
questions.explanation: The sagittal suture runs front to back along the top of your head, joining the two parietal bones.

content.origin: From the Latin word for time. The hair at your temples often turns grey first, showing the passing of time.
content.location: On the right side and base of your skull, all around the right ear, below the parietal bone.
content.description: A busy bone with a thin flat part at the temple, a bump behind the ear and a hollow for the jaw joint. Its ear canal leads inward.
content.function: It holds and protects the parts of the ear for hearing and balance. It also makes the jaw joint with the mandible, so you can chew.
content.mnemonic: Temporal means time to listen. This bone holds your hearing organs.
content.clinical: The pterion, where four skull bones meet at the temple, is thin. A blow here can tear the artery beneath and cause a dangerous bleed outside the brain's lining.
content.hint: The bone around the right ear canal, with a bump behind the ear and a hollow for the jaw joint.

questions.text: The temporal bone forms a joint with which bone so you can chew?
questions.explanation: The jaw bone, the mandible, fits into a hollow in the temporal bone to make the jaw joint.

questions.text: A blow to the thin pterion at the side of the head can tear which artery?
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery runs just under the thin pterion. If it tears, blood collects outside the brain's lining.

content.origin: From the Latin word paries, meaning a wall. The two parietal bones are the side walls of your skull.
content.location: The upper left side and roof of your skull, above the left ear. It sits behind the frontal bone and in front of the occipital bone.
content.description: A big, curved, roughly square plate, like a roof tile. It meets its partner along the top of the head, at the sagittal suture.
content.function: It forms much of the roof and left wall of your skull. It guards the part of the brain that makes sense of touch and space.
content.mnemonic: Picture the two parietal bones as the walls of the brain's house, meeting at the roof ridge.
content.clinical: In babies, the soft spot at the front of the head lies where both parietal bones meet the frontal bone. Doctors check it for sinking or bulging.
content.hint: A large curved plate forming the roof and left side wall of the skull, meeting its partner along the midline seam.

content.origin: From the Latin word for time. The hair at your temples often turns grey first, showing the passing of time.
content.location: On the left side and base of your skull, all around the left ear, below the parietal bone.
content.description: A busy bone with a thin flat part at the temple, a bump behind the ear and a hollow for the jaw joint. Its ear canal leads inward.
content.function: It holds and protects the parts of the ear for hearing and balance. It also makes the jaw joint with the mandible, so you can chew.
content.mnemonic: Temple, time and tympanum, the eardrum. This bone surrounds your ear.
content.clinical: The thin spot at the temple called the pterion covers the middle meningeal artery. A hard knock there can make it bleed and press on the brain.
content.hint: The bone around the left ear canal, with a bump behind the ear and a hollow for the jaw joint.

content.origin: From the Latin word nasus, meaning nose.
content.location: In the upper part of your nose, just right of the middle line. The frontal bone is above it and the right maxilla is beside it.
content.description: A small, thin, oblong bone. It meets its partner in the middle to make the bony bridge of the nose, while the softer lower nose is cartilage.
content.function: It forms the hard bridge of your nose and holds up the bendy cartilage below.
content.mnemonic: The nasal bones are where your glasses rest. Feel the hard bit at the top of your nose.
content.clinical: The nasal bones break more often than any other face bone, usually from a direct knock to the nose.
content.hint: One of the two small bones forming the hard bridge of the nose, where glasses rest.

questions.text: Which face bone is broken most often?
questions.explanation: The nasal bones stick out and are thin, so they break more easily than any other bone of the face.

content.origin: From the Latin word nasus, meaning nose.
content.location: In the upper part of your nose, just left of the middle line. The frontal bone is above it and the left maxilla is beside it.
content.description: A small, thin, oblong bone. It meets its partner in the middle to make the bony bridge of the nose, while the softer lower nose is cartilage.
content.function: It forms the hard bridge of your nose and holds up the bendy cartilage below.
content.mnemonic: Pinch the top of your nose. The hard part is the two nasal bones, the rest is cartilage.
content.clinical: A punch or a ball to the face often breaks the nasal bones. They are the most often broken bones of the face.
content.hint: One of the two small bones forming the hard bridge of the nose, where glasses rest.

content.origin: From the Latin word lacrima, meaning a tear.
content.location: In the inner wall of your right eye socket, near the front, close to the side of your nose.
content.description: The smallest and most fragile bone of the face, about the size of a fingernail. A groove in it holds the tear sac.
content.function: It helps build the inner wall of the eye socket. With the maxilla it houses the tear sac and the start of the duct that drains tears into your nose.
content.mnemonic: Lacrimal means tears. It is the tiny bone where your tears drain away.
content.clinical: If the tear duct is blocked, tears cannot drain into the nose, so the eye waters and may get sticky. This is common in newborns and usually clears up.
content.hint: The smallest face bone, a fingernail-sized plate in the inner wall of the eye socket where tears drain.

questions.text: The name lacrimal refers to what?
questions.explanation: Lacrima is Latin for a tear. The lacrimal bone holds the tear sac.

questions.text: Where is the lacrimal bone found?
options: In the inner wall of the eye socket
questions.explanation: The lacrimal bone sits at the front of the inner wall of the eye socket, next to the nose.

content.origin: From the Latin word lacrima, meaning a tear.
content.location: In the inner wall of your left eye socket, near the front, close to the side of your nose.
content.description: The smallest and most fragile bone of the face, about the size of a fingernail. A groove in it holds the tear sac.
content.function: It helps build the inner wall of the eye socket. With the maxilla it houses the tear sac and the start of the duct that drains tears into your nose.
content.mnemonic: Think lachrymose, a word for tearful. The lacrimal bone is where tears drain.
content.clinical: That is why your nose runs when you cry. A blocked tear duct gives a watery eye, often in newborn babies, and usually clears on its own.
content.hint: The smallest face bone, a fingernail-sized plate in the inner wall of the eye socket where tears drain.

content.origin: From the Greek word for a yoke. With the temporal bone it makes an arch that yokes your face to the side of your skull.
content.location: The high point of your right cheek. It also forms the outer wall and lower outer rim of the right eye socket.
content.description: A roughly diamond-shaped bone. A finger of bone reaches back to join the temporal bone, making the cheekbone arch.
content.function: It shapes your cheek and shields your eye from the side and below. The masseter, a strong chewing muscle, starts from it.
content.mnemonic: Zygomatic means yoke. Your cheekbone yokes your face to your temple.
content.clinical: A hard blow to the cheek can break it in several places. The cheek looks flat, may feel numb, and vision can go double.
content.hint: Find the high point of the right cheek, the bone under the outer rim of the eye socket.

questions.text: The cheekbone arch is made by the zygomatic bone and which other bone?
questions.explanation: A finger of the zygomatic bone meets a finger of the temporal bone. Together they form the zygomatic arch.

content.origin: From the Greek word for a yoke. With the temporal bone it makes an arch that yokes your face to the side of your skull.
content.location: The high point of your left cheek. It also forms the outer wall and lower outer rim of the left eye socket.
content.description: A roughly diamond-shaped bone. A finger of bone reaches back to join the temporal bone, making the cheekbone arch.
content.function: It shapes your cheek and shields your eye from the side and below. The masseter, a strong chewing muscle, starts from it.
content.mnemonic: Run your finger back along your cheekbone toward your ear. That bridge is the zygomatic arch.
content.clinical: A punch to the cheek can crack this bone and its arch. Signs include a flattened cheek, a numb cheek and sometimes double vision.
content.hint: Find the high point of the left cheek, the bone under the outer rim of the eye socket.

content.origin: From the Latin word maxilla, meaning jaw or jawbone.
content.location: The right half of your upper jaw, in the middle of your face. It sits below the right eye socket and beside the nose.
content.description: The two maxillae join in the middle to make the upper jaw. Each holds a row of upper teeth and hides a large air space, the maxillary sinus.
content.function: It holds your upper teeth and forms most of the roof of your mouth. It also makes the floor of the eye socket, so it is called the keystone of the face.
content.mnemonic: The Maxilla holds the upper teeth still, while the Mandible Moves below it.
content.clinical: The maxillary sinus is the biggest sinus of the face. The roots of the upper back teeth sit just under it, so a sinus infection can feel like toothache.
content.hint: The right half of the upper jaw, holding the upper teeth and the largest air space of the face.

questions.text: Which bone holds the upper teeth?
questions.explanation: The maxilla has a ridge of bone, the alveolar process, with sockets for all the upper teeth.

questions.text: Which is the largest sinus of the face?
questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus, inside each maxilla under the eye, is the biggest air space around the nose.

content.origin: From the Latin word maxilla, meaning jaw or jawbone.
content.location: The left half of your upper jaw, in the middle of your face. It sits below the left eye socket and beside the nose.
content.description: The two maxillae join in the middle to make the upper jaw. Each holds a row of upper teeth and hides a large air space, the maxillary sinus.
content.function: It holds your upper teeth and forms most of the roof of your mouth. It also makes the floor of the eye socket, so it is called the keystone of the face.
content.mnemonic: Maxilla is the upper jaw that stays put. The mandible is the lower jaw that moves.
content.clinical: The upper back tooth roots sit right under the biggest face sinus. A tooth infection can spread into it, and sinus pain can feel like toothache.
content.hint: The left half of the upper jaw, holding the upper teeth and the largest air space of the face.

content.origin: From the Latin word palatum, the palate or roof of the mouth.
content.location: At the back of the roof of your mouth and nose, on the right, just behind the right maxilla.
content.description: An L-shaped bone. Its flat part makes the back of the hard palate, and its upright part climbs up the side wall of the nose.
content.function: It finishes off the back of the hard palate, keeping food in your mouth out of your nose. It also helps build the walls of the nose.
content.mnemonic: Palatine means palate. The maxilla makes the front of the roof of your mouth, and the palatine bone finishes the back.
content.clinical: A cleft palate happens when the two halves of the palate do not join before birth. The gap between mouth and nose affects feeding and speech, and surgery repairs it.
content.hint: Look at the very back of the roof of the mouth, on the right, for a small L-shaped bone.

questions.text: The palatine bones form which part of the hard palate?
options: None, they are in the eye socket
questions.explanation: The palatine bones make the back part of the hard palate. The maxillae make the front.

content.origin: From the Latin word palatum, the palate or roof of the mouth.
content.location: At the back of the roof of your mouth and nose, on the left, just behind the left maxilla.
content.description: An L-shaped bone. Its flat part makes the back of the hard palate, and its upright part climbs up the side wall of the nose.
content.function: It finishes off the back of the hard palate, keeping food in your mouth out of your nose. It also helps build the walls of the nose.
content.mnemonic: Run your tongue back along the roof of your mouth. The hard part at the very back is the palatine bone.
content.clinical: If the two sides of the palate fail to join before birth, a baby has a cleft palate. It makes feeding and speech hard, and it is fixed with surgery.
content.hint: Look at the very back of the roof of the mouth, on the left, for a small L-shaped bone.

content.origin: From the Latin word concha, meaning a shell. It is curled like a seashell.
content.location: On the outer wall of the right side of your nose, low down, below the middle concha of the ethmoid.
content.description: A thin, curled scroll of bone. The upper and middle conchae are part of the ethmoid, but this lowest one is a bone of its own.
content.function: It adds surface to the lining of your nose, so the air you breathe in gets warmed, moistened and filtered. The tear duct opens just under it.
content.mnemonic: The lowest shell in the nose is the only one that stands alone as its own bone.
content.clinical: The soft lining over it can swell up with allergies or a cold and block your nose. Very swollen ones are sometimes trimmed by surgery.
content.hint: A separate curled scroll of bone on the lower side wall of the nose.

questions.text: What is the main job of the inferior nasal concha?
options: It warms, moistens and filters air
questions.explanation: Its curled shape adds lining to the nose, which warms, moistens and cleans the air you breathe in.

content.origin: From the Latin word concha, meaning a shell. It is curled like a seashell.
content.location: On the outer wall of the left side of your nose, low down, below the middle concha of the ethmoid.
content.description: A thin, curled scroll of bone. The upper and middle conchae are part of the ethmoid, but this lowest one is a bone of its own.
content.function: It adds surface to the lining of your nose, so the air you breathe in gets warmed, moistened and filtered. The tear duct opens just under it.
content.mnemonic: Picture three shelves of shell in the nose. Only the bottom shelf is a separate bone.
content.clinical: When you have a blocked nose with hay fever, it is mostly the lining over this bone that has swollen up.
content.hint: A separate curled scroll of bone on the lower side wall of the nose.

content.origin: From the Latin word for a ploughshare, the blade of a plough. It is thin and blade-like.
content.location: Right in the middle of your nose, forming the lower back part of the wall between your nostrils.
content.description: A thin, flat plate of bone. Its top edge meets the ethmoid and sphenoid, and its bottom edge rests on the roof of the mouth.
content.function: It helps build the nasal septum, the wall that splits your nose into left and right sides. Cartilage completes the wall at the front.
content.mnemonic: Vomer means ploughshare, a thin blade that ploughs down the middle of your nose.
content.clinical: If the septum bends to one side, it can block one nostril and make breathing hard. This deviated septum can be fixed by an operation.
content.hint: Look down the middle of the nose for a thin blade of bone at the back of the dividing wall.

questions.text: The vomer forms part of which structure?
questions.explanation: The vomer makes the lower back part of the nasal septum, the wall down the middle of your nose.

questions.text: Together with the vomer, which part of the ethmoid makes the bony nasal septum?
questions.explanation: The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid forms the top of the bony septum, and the vomer forms the bottom.

content.origin: From the Latin word mandere, meaning to chew.
content.location: Your lower jaw, forming your chin and lower face. Its upper ends reach up to the temporal bones just in front of your ears.
content.description: The biggest and strongest face bone, shaped like a U. The curved body holds the lower teeth, and an upright branch rises at each end to the jaw joint.
content.function: It holds your lower teeth and is the only skull bone that moves freely. It swings at the jaw joints so you can chew, talk and swallow.
content.mnemonic: Mandible comes from mand, to chew. Remember, the Mandible Moves.
content.clinical: A very wide yawn can pop the jaw joint forward and lock the mouth open. Because the jaw forms a ring with the skull, it often breaks in two places at once.
content.hint: Find the U-shaped bone that holds the lower teeth and moves when you chew.

questions.text: Which skull bone is the only one that moves freely when you chew?
questions.explanation: The mandible swings at the jaw joints, letting you chew and speak.

questions.text: The top end of the mandible, its condyle, forms a joint with which bone?
questions.explanation: The condyle fits into a hollow in the temporal bone, making the jaw joint just in front of your ear.

content.origin: From a Greek word meaning shaped like the letter upsilon, which looks like a U.
content.location: In the front of your neck, under your jaw and just above your voice box. It sits at about the level of C3.
content.description: A small U-shaped bone with a body in front and two pairs of horns. It does not form a joint with any other bone, and muscles hold it in place.
content.function: It anchors your tongue and the floor of your mouth, and it holds up the voice box. It moves up and forward each time you swallow.
content.mnemonic: Hyoid is a floating U that hangs under your jaw. Swallow and feel it rise.
content.clinical: It is well tucked away, so it rarely breaks. A broken hyoid suggests a strong blow or squeeze to the front of the neck.
content.hint: Look in the front of the neck, just under the jaw, for a small U-shaped bone that touches no other bone.

questions.text: What is unusual about the hyoid bone?
options: It is the largest bone of the face
It does not form a joint with any other bone
It contains a large air sinus
questions.explanation: The hyoid floats in the neck, held only by muscles and ligaments. It touches no other bone.

questions.text: The hyoid bone mainly anchors which structure?
questions.explanation: Muscles of the tongue and the floor of the mouth hold on to the hyoid.
